claim_verdicts.evidence: PG17 INSERT, Parameters: "Each column not present in the explicit or implicit column list will be filled with a default value, either its declared default value or null if there is none." Synopsis: INSERT INTO table_name [ ( column_name [, ...] ) ] ... VALUES ( { expression | DEFAULT } [, ...] ) — one expression per named column.

PG17 UPDATE, Description: "UPDATE changes the values of the specified columns in all rows that satisfy the condition." Parameters: "Only rows for which this expression returns true will be updated." PG17 DELETE, Description: the clauses documented are USING, WHERE, WHERE CURRENT OF and RETURNING — there is no SET clause in the DELETE synopsis, and "The optional RETURNING clause causes DELETE to compute and return value(s) based on each row actually deleted."

PG17 6.2 (Updating Data), on the UPDATE WHERE clause: "If it is omitted, it means that all rows in the table are updated. If it is present, only those rows that match the WHERE condition are updated." PG17 DELETE reference: "If the WHERE clause is absent, the effect is to delete all rows in the table. The result is a valid, but empty table." Both describe acceptance, not an error.

The tag forms are right: INSERT Outputs "INSERT oid count … The count is the number of rows inserted or updated. oid is always 0"; UPDATE "UPDATE count"; DELETE "DELETE count … the number of rows deleted". But the restriction to statements returning no rows is contradicted by the protocol page's CommandComplete list: "For a SELECT or CREATE TABLE AS command, the tag is SELECT rows where rows is the number of rows retrieved." Every command returns a tag; what differs is that psql shows a tuple result as a table with a "(n rows)" footer.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: Every statement ends with a command tag; psql shows it under statements whose result is not a table: 'UPDATE n' and 'DELETE n' give the number of rows affected, and 'INSERT 0 n' has an oid field that is always 0 followed by that number. A SELECT also has a tag, but psql prints its rows and a '(n rows)' footer instead.

claim_verdicts.evidence: PG17 INSERT Outputs: "If the INSERT command contains a RETURNING clause, the result will be similar to that of a SELECT statement containing the columns and values defined in the RETURNING list, computed over the row(s) inserted or updated by the command." UPDATE: "The optional RETURNING clause causes UPDATE to compute and return value(s) based on each row actually updated." DELETE: same sentence for "each row actually deleted". Columns filled by the table's identity default are available to RETURNING (INSERT Parameters, default values).

First half verified: UPDATE "changes the values of the specified columns in all rows that satisfy the condition"; DELETE "If the WHERE clause is absent, the effect is to delete all rows in the table." The absolute is not: PG17 ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT — "Roll back all commands that were executed after the savepoint was established and then start a new subtransaction at the same transaction level" — is a second undo the database itself offers, and no page consulted says ROLLBACK is the only one.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: In PostgreSQL 17 an UPDATE or DELETE affects exactly the rows its WHERE keeps, and runs without asking first. Afterwards the undo the database offers is a ROLLBACK of the surrounding transaction (or a ROLLBACK to a savepoint inside it); outside a transaction the statement commits on its own, and the old values have to be put back by hand or restored from a backup.

claim_verdicts.evidence: PG17 5.5.5 Foreign Keys: "NO ACTION means that if any referencing rows still exist when the constraint is checked, an error is raised; this is the default behavior if you do not specify anything", and the same list gives CASCADE ("row(s) referencing it should be automatically deleted as well") and SET NULL. A statement that raises an error applies nothing: PG17 3.4 says each statement outside an explicit transaction has an implicit BEGIN and, if successful, COMMIT wrapped around it.

db/schema.sql l.5: "id integer GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY". db/seed.sql l.71: "SELECT setval(pg_get_serial_sequence('products', 'id'), 8);". PG17 9.17: "The two-parameter form sets the sequence's last_value field to the specified value and sets its is_called field to true, meaning that the next nextval will advance the sequence before returning a value." write-basics.sql l.10-12 omits id, so the identity default supplies the next value: 9.

claim_verdicts.evidence: PG17 9.17: "the value obtained by nextval is not reclaimed for re-use if the calling transaction later aborts. This means that transaction aborts or database crashes can result in gaps in the sequence of assigned values" and "sequence state changes made by setval are immediately visible to other transactions, and are not undone if the calling transaction rolls back." write-basics.sql l.37 is SELECT setval(…, 8), a SELECT returning one bigint, which psql prints as a one-row table (\pset footer on by default).
db/seed.sql l.24, l.25 and l.33: ( 1, 1, …), ( 2, 1, …) and (10, 1, …) — orders 1, 2 and 10 carry customer_id 1, and no other row in l.23-35 references customer 1.

db/schema.sql l.20: "customer_id integer NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id)" — no ON DELETE clause appears anywhere in schema.sql. PG17 5.5.5: "NO ACTION means that if any referencing rows still exist when the constraint is checked, an error is raised; this is the default behavior if you do not specify anything." The handler name used at write-basics.sql l.28 is the condition name for that error class.

PG17 43.9: NOTICE is one of the RAISE levels, and levels other than EXCEPTION "only generate messages of different priority levels"; "Inside the format string, % is replaced by the string representation of the next optional argument's value." PG17 43.6.8: "The special variable SQLERRM contains the error message associated with the exception", and a block with an EXCEPTION clause traps the error so execution continues after it.

ROLLBACK at write-basics.sql l.21 discards the INSERT (l.10-12) and the DELETE (l.18-19); the DO block's DELETE at l.27 is undone by its own handler — PG17 43.6.8: "When an error is caught by an EXCEPTION clause … all changes to persistent database state within the block are rolled back." So at l.33 products still holds the 8 rows of db/seed.sql l.5-13. Derived, not run.

Line 16 of write-basics.sql is "WHERE name = 'Giá đỡ laptop';"; replacing it with a bare ';' leaves "UPDATE products SET price_vnd = 300000 ;", a complete statement, so ON_ERROR_STOP (run-query.sh l.10) is not triggered. PG17 6.2: with WHERE omitted "all rows in the table are updated". At l.14 the table holds the 8 seeded rows plus the row inserted at l.10-12 inside the open transaction; 300000 passes CHECK (price_vnd > 0), so 9 rows change and the tag is UPDATE 9. Derived, not run.

claim_verdicts.evidence: scripts/up.sh exists at stage-0. scripts/sql/run-query.sh l.7-11: query="${1:-select-basics}" then psql --host db --username donhang --dbname donhang --no-psqlrc --echo-queries --set ON_ERROR_STOP=on --file "/repo/db/queries/${query}.sql" — the argument names the file under db/queries and --echo-queries echoes each statement, as the captured outputs/stage-0/scripts/sql/run-query.txt shows for select-basics.

PG17 UPDATE: "UPDATE changes the values of the specified columns in all rows that satisfy the condition", and Outputs: the count is "the number of rows updated, including matched rows whose values did not change" — so the tag counts the matched set. DELETE: "the number of rows deleted". The same WHERE over the same table therefore selects the same set in both statements; the claim's own condition ("nothing else writes to it in between") covers the concurrent case.

issues.text: Unlisted claim: whether an uncaught error stops the file is not a property of PostgreSQL but of the lab's psql invocation. scripts/sql/run-query.sh l.10 passes --set ON_ERROR_STOP=on; with psql's default the error would be reported and the remaining statements would still run, so the sentence is false outside this script. PG17 psql documents the flag ('execution of the remaining queries continues unless ON_ERROR_STOP is set'; exit code '3 if an error occurred in a script and the variable ON_ERROR_STOP was set'). No claim covers it - claim 19 stops at --echo-queries.
issues.quote: Without the block around it, the refusal would stop the file with an error
issues.fix: Name the cause and add it to the ledger: "Without the block around it, the refusal would stop the run, because the lab's script tells psql to stop at the first error." Add a claim citing scripts/sql/run-query.sh l.10 (--set ON_ERROR_STOP=on) and the psql page.

A reader who applies §5 and q5 correctly concludes no option does the job, so the key is right only as a statement shape, not as an outcome.
issues.quote: `DELETE FROM products WHERE name = 'Đèn bàn LED';` — `DELETE` removes whole rows, so it has no `SET`
issues.fix: Point the question at the row nothing references: change the stem (en and vi) to the laptop bag the `INSERT` just added — "The shop decides the `Túi đựng laptop` row the `INSERT` just added should go again" — and make options a, c and d use name = 'Túi đựng laptop'. issues.text: The definition restricts command tags to statements that return no rows. PG17's CommandComplete list gives a tag for every command, SELECT included: "For a SELECT or CREATE TABLE AS command, the tag is SELECT rows where rows is the number of rows retrieved." What is true is that psql shows a tuple result as a table with a "(n rows)" footer rather than the tag. Claim 5 carries the same over-restriction and is rephrased above.
issues.quote: the short answer PostgreSQL returns for a statement that produces no rows, which psql shows under it, such as `UPDATE 1`
issues.fix: Rewrite the bullet: "command tag — the short answer PostgreSQL returns for every statement; psql shows it under the ones whose result is not a table, such as `UPDATE 1`, and it gives the number of rows the statement touched."

issues.text: Carried over from r2 and not applied. "every change" is contradicted twelve lines later by §5 ("takes all three changes back, except the counter — a rollback does not wind that back") and by PG17 9.17: "sequence state changes made by setval are immediately visible to other transactions, and are not undone if the calling transaction rolls back." Claim 13 says only that row changes come back.
issues.quote: the only undo the database itself offers is a `ROLLBACK`: it takes back every change made since the matching `BEGIN`
issues.fix: One word: "…is a `ROLLBACK`: it takes back every row change made since the matching `BEGIN`, which is why the lab file opens one." §5's exception then stops contradicting §4.

issues.text: Carried over from r2 and not applied; two absolutes in one paragraph ("the only undo the database itself offers", "only writing the old values back undoes it"). PG17 offers a second in-database undo — ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT: "Roll back all commands that were executed after the savepoint was established" — and in the §2 shop scenario restoring a backup is the usual answer to a committed mistake. Claim 7 stops at "outside one, the statement commits on its own".
issues.quote: Outside such a pair the change stands, and only writing the old values back undoes it.
issues.fix: Drop the absolute: "Outside such a pair the change stands, and getting the old values back means writing them back yourself or restoring a backup."

issues.text: The numbered list is presented as what the run prints "in this order", but it omits the `INSERT 0 1` tag that §4 itself tells the reader to expect after an INSERT: psql prints the RETURNING table and the command status (PG17 psql notes suppression only for \copy … to stdout). The reader comparing the screen with the list finds a line that is not in it, right at the step where the id 9 is checked. Not run (no Docker engine), so the exact spacing is undetermined; the tag's presence is documented.

2. the inserted row, with `id` 9;

issues.text: Carried over from r2 and not applied. Option b's explanation says PostgreSQL "aims it at all eight rows" and only afterwards adds the hedge "in a table nothing references"; in the lab every product 1-8 appears in db/seed.sql l.37-49, so DELETE FROM products; is refused by the order_items foreign key of db/schema.sql l.28. Quiz question 4 asks me to reject "Naming `id` there is what tells PostgreSQL to fill the column in", and that needs exactly this distinction.
